sections.html: After the examination and CT scan we share, item by item and in writing, what will be done to each tooth, the implant brand and crown material, and any additional procedures. If you send your X-rays and photos via WhatsApp we can give preliminary information. For the stages of treatment, see our step-by-step implant guide.

faq.q: Does the implant price include the crown?
faq.a: It depends on the clinic. Some prices cover only the implant screw, with the abutment and crown charged separately. Ask for these items to be listed separately in any quote.

faq.q: Why are implants in Türkiye often less expensive?
faq.a: Lower operating and laboratory costs are the main reasons. Quality depends on the clinic, the materials and the dentist, not the country, so compare written plans rather than headline prices.

faq.q: Can I pay in stages?
faq.a: We discuss payment options based on the plan after the examination. Because treatment spans months, payments can usually follow the treatment stages.

faq.q: Is a single implant or a bridge more economical?
faq.a: A bridge can look cheaper in the short term, but it requires reducing the neighbouring teeth and may need replacing later. See our implant or bridge article for a comparison.

title: Types of dental crowns: zirconia, e.max, porcelain and veneers compared
desc: What a dental crown is and when it's needed. The differences between zirconia, e.max (glass ceramic), porcelain-fused-to-metal and laminate veneers, how long they last and how to choose.
lead: A dental crown is a restoration that fully covers and protects a worn, broken, discoloured or root-filled tooth. The most common options are zirconia, e.max glass ceramic and porcelain fused to metal; a laminate veneer covers only the front surface and removes less tooth structure.

sections.html:
• Teeth weakened by large fillings
  • Broken or cracked teeth
  • After root canal treatment, especially back teeth
  • Severe discolouration that whitening can't lift
  • Teeth supporting a bridge, and teeth on implants
  • Comprehensive correction of shape and size

TypeAestheticsStrengthTypical use
ZirconiaNatural-looking, metal-freeVery highFront and back teeth, bridges, on implants
E.max (lithium disilicate)Very high translucencyHighFront teeth, single crowns, veneers
Porcelain fused to metalGood, but more opaqueHigh, long clinical track recordBack teeth, long bridges
Laminate veneerVery highHigh in the right caseFront surface of front teeth

We compare zirconia and porcelain in zirconia or porcelain, explain e.max in what are e.max crowns, and cover veneers in our laminate veneer guide.

sections.h: Which crown is right for you?
sections.html:
The choice depends on how much healthy tooth remains, where the tooth is, your bite force, whether you grind your teeth, your gum level and your aesthetic goals. Translucency matters most at the front; fracture resistance matters most at the back.

If a tooth is healthy and only its colour or shape needs changing, more conservative options such as veneers or bonding should be considered first. Unnecessary full crowns sacrifice healthy tooth structure.

Important

Crowns shouldn't be the first choice for "whiter teeth". If colour is the only issue, teeth whitening is considered first.

StageWhat happens
Examination and planningX-rays, smile design if needed, shade selection
Tooth preparationUnder local anaesthetic, the tooth is reduced by the thickness of the crown
ImpressionDigital scan or conventional impression; temporary crowns fitted
Try-inFit, shade and shape checked
CementationThe final crown is bonded and the bite checked

In most cases treatment is completed within 1–2 weeks. The number of visits depends on how many teeth are treated and whether other treatment is needed.

Well-planned, well-maintained crowns last ten years or more for most patients. The biggest threats are decay at the margins, gum disease and grinding. For sensitivity and care after crowns, see our aftercare guide. You can read about crown options at our Beylikdüzü clinic in the treatments section.

faq.q: How much is the tooth reduced for a crown?
faq.a: It depends on the material, typically around 1–2 mm. For a veneer, only 0.3–0.7 mm is removed from the front surface, sometimes none.

faq.q: Can a crowned tooth decay?
faq.a: The crown itself can't decay, but the tooth underneath can, especially at the gum line. That's why flossing and regular check-ups matter.

faq.q: Can crowns be whitened?
faq.a: No. Crowns, fillings and veneers don't change colour with whitening. If you're considering whitening, do it before your crowns are made.

faq.q: Does a root-filled tooth need a crown?
faq.a: Back teeth are more prone to fracture after root canal treatment, so a crown is often recommended. Front teeth and teeth with little tissue loss may only need a filling.

title: Root canal treatment: when is it needed, how many visits, does it hurt?
desc: What root canal treatment is, the symptoms that call for it, how many visits it takes and whether it hurts. Pain afterwards, whether a crown is needed, and why saving the tooth matters.
lead: Root canal treatment cleans out a nerve (pulp) inflamed by decay or trauma, disinfects the canals and seals them. It's done under local anaesthetic, usually takes 1–2 visits, and aims to keep the tooth rather than extract it.

sections.h: Symptoms that may mean you need a root canal
sections.html:
• Pain after hot or cold that lingers
  • Spontaneous, throbbing pain that wakes you at night
  • Tenderness when biting or touching the tooth
  • Swelling of the gum or a pimple-like bump that discharges
  • Darkening of the tooth (especially after an injury)

Sometimes a nerve dies without any symptoms and is found on a routine X-ray, which is why regular check-ups matter.

sections.h: How is root canal treatment done?
sections.html:
1. X-rays show the number and length of roots and the extent of infection.
  2. Local anaesthetic is given and the tooth is isolated.
  3. Decay is removed and the nerve tissue is reached.
  4. The canals are cleaned and shaped with special instruments and rinsed with disinfecting solutions.
  5. The canals are filled with a sealing material.
  6. The tooth is restored with a permanent filling or crown.

sections.h: How many visits does it take?
sections.html:
SituationTypical visits
Vital but inflamed nerveUsually one
Dead nerve with infection at the root (abscess)Usually two, with medication placed in between
Redoing a previous root canalTwo or more

A visit usually lasts 45–90 minutes. Front teeth have fewer canals and take less time; molars take longer.

It's done under local anaesthetic and most patients feel no significant pain during treatment. In fact, it relieves the pain caused by the inflammation. Mild tenderness when biting for a few days afterwards is common and usually settles with simple painkillers.

When to call

If swelling increases, if pain gets worse rather than better over a few days, or if you develop a fever, contact the clinic.

sections.h: Do I need a crown after a root canal?
sections.html: Root-filled teeth, especially back teeth, are more prone to fracture because of lost tooth structure, so a crown is often recommended for molars. Front teeth or teeth with little tissue loss may only need a filling. See types of dental crowns.

Extraction can look quicker in the short term, but the missing tooth then needs replacing with an implant or bridge, which takes longer and costs more. Keeping the natural tooth is usually the first choice when possible. If a tooth has been lost, see implant or bridge. You can also read more in our treatments section.

faq.q: Can a root canal be done in one visit?
faq.a: If the nerve is still vital and there's no infection at the root, often yes. With an abscess, it's usually completed in two visits.

faq.q: How long does pain last after a root canal?
faq.a: Mild tenderness usually fades over 2–5 days. Increasing pain or swelling should be checked.

faq.q: How long does a root-filled tooth last?
faq.a: A well-treated and properly restored root-filled tooth can last many years, often for life.

faq.q: Can I have a root canal while pregnant?
faq.a: Yes, when needed; the second trimester is usually the most comfortable time. X-rays and medication are planned with your pregnancy in mind.

title: Implant or bridge? Which is better for a missing tooth?
desc: Implant or bridge for a missing tooth? A comparison of the effect on neighbouring teeth, bone loss, treatment time, cleaning, lifespan and cost.
lead: There are two fixed ways to replace a missing tooth: an implant placed in the jawbone, or a bridge supported by the neighbouring teeth. An implant leaves the neighbouring teeth untouched and helps preserve bone; a bridge is quicker but may require reducing healthy teeth.

sections.h: The key differences between an implant and a bridge
sections.html:
FeatureImplantBridge
Neighbouring teethUntouchedSupporting teeth are reduced
BoneTransfers chewing load to bone, slowing shrinkageBone under the gap continues to shrink
TimeUsually 3–6 monthsUsually 1–2 weeks
SurgeryMinor surgery neededNo surgery
CleaningBrush and floss like a natural toothSpecial floss or interdental brush under the bridge
Initial costUsually higherUsually lower

sections.h: When does an implant make more sense?
sections.html:
• When the teeth either side of the gap are healthy and unfilled: there's no reason to reduce them for a bridge.
  • When there's enough bone, or bone can be built up with a graft.
  • When you want a long-term, independent solution: if a problem ever arises with an implant, the neighbouring teeth aren't affected.
  • When several teeth in a row are missing and there aren't enough supporting teeth for a bridge.

For the stages and timeline, see how long implant treatment takes.

sections.h: When might a bridge be the better choice?
sections.html:
• When the neighbouring teeth already have large fillings or need crowns anyway: the bridge protects them at the same time.
  • When general health doesn't allow surgery.
  • When bone is very limited and the patient doesn't want extra surgery.
  • When treatment needs to be completed quickly.

Our article on types of dental crowns explains the materials used for bridges.

Both can last many years when well planned and properly cared for. With bridges, the most common problems are decay starting at the crown margins of the supporting teeth and gum problems, so cleaning under the bridge is essential. With implants, the main risk is inflammation of the gum and bone around the implant (peri-implantitis).

Over the long term implants usually have the edge, because even if the crown is replaced the implant itself can stay in place.

Important

Leaving a gap for a long time can let the opposing tooth over-erupt into the space and the neighbouring teeth tip into it. Whichever option you choose, it's best not to wait too long.

The decision depends on the neighbouring teeth, bone volume, general health, budget and expectations. At the examination we explain both options with their pros and cons and compare them in writing. Get in touch to book an appointment.

faq.q: Can I switch from a bridge to an implant later?
faq.a: Yes. The bridge can be removed and an implant placed in the gap; but because the supporting teeth were reduced, they will need crowns too. Bone is assessed separately.

faq.q: Which is recommended for a single missing tooth?
faq.a: If the teeth on either side are healthy, an implant is usually recommended because no healthy tooth structure is removed. If the neighbouring teeth need crowns anyway, a bridge can also be suitable.

faq.q: What is an implant bridge?
faq.a: When several teeth are missing, a bridge is made on two or more implants instead of placing one implant per tooth. Natural teeth aren't touched.

faq.q: Is a removable denture also an option?
faq.a: Yes. Partial dentures cost less but offer less comfort and chewing efficiency than fixed solutions.

title: Toothache at night or at the weekend: what to do and when it's urgent
desc: What you can do at home for toothache that starts in the evening or at the weekend, which situations are urgent, broken teeth, lost crowns, facial swelling and a dentist open at weekends in Beylikdüzü, Istanbul.
lead: When toothache starts, first judge how severe it is and whether there's swelling or fever. Swelling spreading to the face or neck, difficulty swallowing or breathing, and a high temperature are emergencies; otherwise, painkillers and cold compresses can bring relief until you're seen.

sections.html:
SituationWhat to do
Swelling spreading to the face, under the eye or neck, with feverSee a dentist the same day; if swallowing or breathing is difficult, go to hospital A&E immediately
A permanent tooth knocked outHold it by the crown, not the root, keep it in milk and see a dentist as soon as possible (ideally within an hour)
Bleeding that won't stop (after extraction)Press with gauze for 30 minutes; if it continues, call the clinic or go to A&E
Throbbing pain that keeps you awakePainkiller and the earliest available appointment
Broken tooth, lost filling or crownIf there's no pain, an appointment within a few days

sections.h: What can you do at home until you're seen?
sections.html:
• Take a painkiller you've used before and that suits you, at the dose on the leaflet.
  • If there's swelling, apply cold to the outside of the cheek; don't apply heat.
  • If food is stuck between teeth, remove it gently with floss.
  • Rinse gently with warm salt water.
  • Avoid chewing on that side and avoid very hot, cold or sugary foods.
What not to do

Don't place painkiller tablets on the tooth or gum; they burn the tissue. Don't take antibiotics without a prescription; unless the source of infection is treated, the problem comes back.

SymptomPossible cause
Brief twinge with coldSensitivity, exposed root or small cavity
Lingering pain made worse by heatNerve inflammation; root canal treatment may be needed
Pain on bitingInfection at the root, cracked tooth or high filling
Pain at the back with limited mouth openingInflammation around a wisdom tooth
Gum swelling with dischargeAbscess

Nerve inflammation and abscesses often need root canal treatment; for pain from wisdom teeth, see our wisdom tooth guide.

sections.h: Broken tooth or lost crown: what to do
sections.html:
If you can find the broken piece, keep it in a clean container; on front teeth it can sometimes be bonded back. If a sharp edge irritates your tongue or cheek, cover it with sugar-free gum or orthodontic wax.

Don't glue a lost crown back yourself. Keep it and call the clinic. For other crown problems, see our guide to care after crowns.

sections.h: A dentist open at weekends in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
Dent32 sees patients seven days a week at its clinic on the E-5 service road in Beylikdüzü. For toothache that starts in the evening or at the weekend, message us on WhatsApp for the earliest available time. Sending a photo and describing your symptoms helps us prioritise. Find our contact details here.

If facial swelling is growing quickly or you have difficulty swallowing or breathing, go straight to the nearest hospital emergency department.

faq.q: Does toothache go away on its own?
faq.a: The pain can ease temporarily, but that doesn't mean the problem is solved. A dying nerve can stop hurting while infection continues at the root. Even if the pain goes, get it checked.

faq.q: Are antibiotics enough for a dental abscess?
faq.a: Antibiotics can help control spreading infection but don't remove the cause. A lasting solution needs root canal treatment or extraction.

faq.q: Which painkiller should I take for toothache at night?
faq.a: You can take a painkiller you've used before and that suits you, at the dose on the leaflet. If you have a chronic condition, are pregnant or take regular medication, ask a pharmacist.

faq.q: Can I get a weekend appointment?
faq.a: Yes. Our clinic is open seven days a week; message us on WhatsApp for an available time.

title: What are e.max crowns? How they differ from zirconia and who they suit
desc: What e.max (lithium disilicate glass ceramic) crowns are and how they compare with zirconia: aesthetics, strength, uses, lifespan and when they're the right choice.
lead: E.max is a highly translucent crown material made from a glass ceramic called lithium disilicate. It stands out for its natural look on front teeth; because it's slightly less strong than zirconia, it's chosen with care for back teeth and for people who grind.

sections.html:
E.max is a glass ceramic system for metal-free, all-ceramic restorations. It transmits and reflects light very much like natural enamel, so it blends well with neighbouring natural teeth, especially at the front.

It can be made as crowns, laminate veneers, inlays and onlays. Because it's bonded to the tooth surface (adhesive cementation), it can be made thin, allowing less tooth structure to be removed.

FeatureE.maxZirconia
TranslucencyVery highHigh (improved in newer zirconias)
Fracture resistanceHighVery high
Minimum thicknessCan be made thinUsually needs a little more thickness
BridgesLimited to short front bridgesSuitable for long bridges and implants
Typical useFront teeth, veneers, single crownsBack teeth, bridges, on implants

For zirconia versus porcelain fused to metal, see zirconia or porcelain.

• People with colour, shape or small chip problems on front teeth
  • Smile design cases where a natural look is the top priority
  • Situations where minimal tooth removal is wanted (veneers, inlays and onlays)

For people who grind at night, or in back teeth with heavy chewing forces, zirconia is usually the safer choice. If you grind, a night guard is recommended whatever the material.

Used in the right case and well bonded, e.max restorations last for many years. The key factors are case selection, controlling grinding and oral hygiene. See our guide to sensitivity and care after crowns.

In short

For the most natural look on front teeth, e.max; for back teeth, bridges or grinders, zirconia is usually more suitable. The decision is made at the examination and as part of the smile plan.
Smile design cases often combine both: e.max at the front and zirconia at the back, balancing aesthetics and strength. See our smile design guide, or compare all options in types of dental crowns.

faq.q: E.max or veneers?
faq.a: A veneer is a type of restoration; e.max is a material. Veneers are often made from e.max glass ceramic. How much of the tooth is covered (front only or all of it) depends on the tooth's condition.

faq.q: Can e.max break?
faq.a: Fractures are rare when the case is right and the thickness is adequate. Grinding, biting hard objects (pens, seeds, ice) and insufficient thickness raise the risk.

faq.q: Does e.max stain?
faq.a: No. The glass ceramic surface resists staining from tea, coffee and smoking. Any staining at the edges can usually be polished away.

faq.q: Can e.max be used on back teeth?
faq.a: It can be used for single crowns on back teeth, but with heavy bite forces or grinding, zirconia is usually safer.

title: After dental implant surgery: eating, drinking, smoking and care
desc: What to do after implant surgery: the first 24 hours, swelling and pain, what to eat and when, smoking, exercise, brushing and long-term implant care.
lead: In the first 24 hours after implant surgery, cold compresses, soft lukewarm food, leaving the area alone and not smoking all help healing. Over the long term, regular cleaning and check-ups are what most determine how long an implant lasts.

sections.html:
• Gauze: Bite on the gauze provided for 30–45 minutes.
  • Cold compress: Apply ice to the outside of the cheek for 15–20 minutes at a time.
  • Eating: Don't eat until the numbness wears off; then choose soft, lukewarm food.
  • Rinsing: Avoid vigorous rinsing and spitting on the first day so the clot isn't disturbed.
  • Straws: Don't use them; the suction can increase bleeding.
  • Medication: Take the prescribed painkillers and, if given, antibiotics as directed.

sections.h: What can I eat, and when?
sections.html:
PeriodRecommendedAvoid
First 2–3 daysYoghurt, lukewarm soup, mash, puddings, soft omeletteHot drinks, hard or spicy food, alcohol
First 1–2 weeksPasta, rice, cooked vegetables, fish, meatballsNuts, crusty bread, seeds
While the implant healsNormal diet, chewing on the other sidePutting heavy load directly on the implant

sections.h: Are swelling, bruising and pain normal?
sections.html:
Yes. Swelling usually peaks on day 2 or 3 and then subsides. Mild bruising on the cheek can appear, especially after several implants or a bone graft, and fades within a week. Pain is usually controlled with simple painkillers.

When to call the clinic

If bleeding doesn't stop despite gauze, swelling and pain increase after day 3, you have a rising temperature, a bad taste or discharge, or numbness hasn't worn off by the next day.

sections.h: Can I smoke after an implant?
sections.html: Smoking reduces blood flow in the gum and bone, slows healing and significantly increases the risk of the implant failing to fuse. Avoid smoking completely for at least the first 48–72 hours, and ideally throughout the healing period. We cover how smoking and diabetes affect implants in who can get dental implants.

On the day of surgery you can gently brush the teeth away from the surgical site. From the next day, clean the surgical area carefully with a soft brush. If advised, use lukewarm salt water or an antiseptic mouthwash.

Stitches are usually removed after 7–10 days or dissolve on their own.

sections.h: Long term: how to look after an implant
sections.html:
• Brush twice a day and use an interdental brush or floss around the implant
  • A check-up and professional clean every six months
  • A night guard if you grind or clench
  • Prompt check-up if you notice bleeding gums

Implants can't decay, but the gum and bone around them can become inflamed (peri-implantitis). Caught early, it's much easier to treat. See our articles on bleeding gums and night guards.

faq.q: When can I exercise after an implant?
faq.a: Avoid strenuous exercise for the first 3–5 days, as raised blood pressure can increase bleeding. Light walking is fine from the next day.

faq.q: Can I drink coffee after an implant?
faq.a: Avoid hot drinks on the first day. From the following days, lukewarm coffee is fine.

faq.q: Are antibiotics always needed after an implant?
faq.a: Not for every patient. Whether antibiotics are needed depends on the extent of surgery and your health, and is decided by the dentist.

faq.q: How do I know if the implant has taken?
faq.a: During healing an implant usually gives no symptoms. It's checked clinically and with X-rays at follow-ups, and its stability is confirmed before the final tooth is fitted.

title: Bleeding and receding gums: causes and treatment
desc: Why gums bleed and recede. Signs of gingivitis and periodontitis, scaling, root planing, treatment for gum recession and home care.
lead: Gums that bleed when you brush are usually the first sign of gum inflammation caused by plaque and tartar. Caught early, it reverses completely with a professional clean and good home care; left untreated, it can progress to periodontitis, which affects the bone that holds the teeth.

sections.html:
Bacterial plaque building up on the teeth inflames the gums. Inflamed gums become red and swollen and bleed easily when brushing or flossing. When plaque hardens it becomes tartar, which a toothbrush can no longer remove.

  • Inadequate brushing and no flossing
  • Tartar
  • Smoking (which can mask bleeding and hide the disease)
  • Pregnancy and hormonal changes
  • Diabetes
  • Some medications, including blood thinners

Gingivitis (gum inflammation)Periodontitis (advanced gum disease)
Tissue affectedGums onlyGums and the bone holding the teeth
SignsRedness, swelling, bleedingRecession, bad breath, loose or spreading teeth
Reversible?Fully reversibleLost bone usually doesn't return; the disease is halted
TreatmentProfessional clean and home careDeep cleaning, root planing, surgery if needed

The most common causes of recession are periodontitis and brushing too hard. Grinding, thin gum tissue, orthodontic movement and tight lip or cheek attachments can contribute. Recession exposes the root surface, which can lead to sensitivity, root decay and cosmetic concerns.

Brushing

Use a soft-bristled brush and avoid a horizontal sawing motion. Angle the brush at 45 degrees to the gum and use small circular movements.

1. Examination, gum pocket measurements and X-rays to assess bone level
  2. Scaling and polishing
  3. Root planing under local anaesthetic if needed
  4. Re-assessment after 4–8 weeks
  5. Surgical procedures such as flap surgery or gum grafts in advanced cases
  6. Regular maintenance (usually every 3–6 months)

We answer common questions about scaling in our article on professional teeth cleaning.

sections.h: Why gum health affects other treatments
sections.html: The long-term success of implants, crowns and orthodontics depends on healthy gums. A similar inflammation (peri-implantitis) can develop around implants. That's why gum disease is treated first. Read more in our treatments section or book an appointment at our Beylikdüzü clinic.

faq.q: My gums bleed. Should I stop brushing?
faq.a: No. Bleeding is a sign of inflammation; gentle but regular brushing and flossing help it settle. If it doesn't improve in a week or two, see a dentist.

faq.q: Do receded gums grow back?
faq.a: Not on their own. In suitable cases, procedures such as gum grafts can cover the root again. The cause of the recession is addressed first.

faq.q: Can bad breath come from gum disease?
faq.a: Yes, gum disease and bacteria on the tongue are among the most common causes of persistent bad breath.

faq.q: Is bleeding gums normal in pregnancy?
faq.a: It's common because of hormonal changes (pregnancy gingivitis). A check-up and a clean are still recommended; scaling is safe during pregnancy.

title: Bone grafts and sinus lifts: can I have implants with too little bone?
desc: What bone grafts and sinus lifts are, when they're needed, whether they hurt and how much they extend implant treatment. Open versus closed sinus lift.
lead: If the jawbone isn't wide or tall enough to hold an implant, a bone graft is used to build it up; in the upper back jaw, the sinus floor can be raised (sinus lift) to make room. These procedures often make implants possible, but they lengthen treatment.

sections.html:
Once a tooth is lost, the bone that held it no longer receives chewing load and gradually becomes thinner and shorter. Most of this loss happens in the first months after extraction. Advanced gum disease, long-term use of removable dentures and trauma can also cause bone loss.

The upper back jaw has an extra issue: after teeth are lost, the sinus can expand downwards, reducing the bone height left for an implant.

A bone graft is a material that acts as scaffolding for new bone. It can be the patient's own bone, processed human or animal bone, or a synthetic material. It's usually covered with a membrane and is gradually replaced by the patient's own bone over a few months.

UseWhen?
Filling the extraction socket (socket preservation)At extraction, to limit bone loss if an implant is planned
Graft at the same time as the implantFor small bone defects
Graft first, implant laterWhen bone is very thin; the implant usually follows 4–6 months later

In a sinus lift, the membrane lining the floor of the sinus in the upper back jaw is gently raised and bone graft material is placed beneath it, creating the bone height needed for an implant.

TechniqueWhen it's usedFeatures
Closed (internal) sinus liftWhen moderate bone height remainsDone through the implant site, usually with the implant at the same visit
Open (lateral) sinus liftWhen very little bone remainsA small window is made from the side; the implant is placed at the same visit or months later

Both are done under local anaesthetic. Swelling and mild bruising afterwards can be a little more noticeable than after a simple implant and usually settle within a week. For two weeks after a sinus lift, avoid blowing your nose, sneeze with your mouth open, and check with your dentist before flying.

After a sinus lift

Don't blow your nose forcefully, sneeze with your mouth open, and avoid strenuous exercise and diving. A little nosebleed on the first day can be normal.

sections.h: How much longer does treatment take?
sections.html: Small grafts placed with the implant usually add little time. A separate graft or open sinus lift can add 3–6 months overall. For the general timeline, see how long implant treatment takes; for the effect on cost, see what affects implant cost.

In some cases short implants, angled implants or techniques such as All-on-Four avoid the need for extra bone surgery. Which route suits you is decided from the CT scan. For full-arch solutions, see our All-on-Four guide.

faq.q: Can the body reject a bone graft?
faq.a: Graft materials are biocompatible and aren't rejected in the classic sense. Rarely, infection or incomplete bone formation can occur; the procedure can then be repeated.

faq.q: Can a sinus lift cause sinusitis?
faq.a: When properly planned, a sinus lift doesn't cause sinusitis. Chronic sinusitis is assessed beforehand, with an ENT opinion if needed.

faq.q: Should a graft be placed when a tooth is extracted?
faq.a: If an implant is planned for that site, grafting the socket can reduce bone loss. The decision depends on the tooth's position and the bone.

faq.q: How long after a graft is the implant placed?
faq.a: For separate grafts, usually 4–6 months. Small grafts can be done at the same visit as the implant.

title: When should your child first see a dentist?
desc: When a child's first dental visit should be, baby tooth decay, fluoride varnish, fissure sealants, preventing dental anxiety and tips for children's oral care.
lead: A child's first dental visit should be when the first baby tooth appears, or by their first birthday at the latest. Early, relaxed visits help prevent decay and let children build a relationship of trust with the dentist.

sections.html:
Baby teeth can decay as soon as they come through. "Bottle decay" can progress quickly, especially in babies who drink milk or juice from a bottle at night. At the first visit the teeth are checked and parents get advice on brushing, diet and dummy use.

This visit is usually short and involves no treatment; the aim is for the child to get to know the surroundings and for any risks to be spotted early.

TreatmentWhat it doesWhen
Fluoride varnishStrengthens enamel and increases resistance to decay2–4 times a year depending on risk
Fissure sealantsSeal the deep grooves on the biting surfaces of molarsUsually around ages 6 and 12, when permanent molars erupt
Regular check-upsCatch decay while it's smallUsually every 6 months

sections.h: Baby teeth fall out anyway. Do they need treating?
sections.html:
Yes. Baby teeth aren't only for chewing and speaking; they also hold space for the permanent teeth. Losing them early can cause crowding. Untreated decay in baby teeth can lead to pain, abscesses and damage to the permanent tooth underneath.

Space maintainers

If a baby tooth has to be removed early, a space maintainer can keep the gap open until the permanent tooth comes through.

sections.h: How to prevent fear of the dentist
sections.html:
• Make the first visit a check-up, before there's any pain.
  • Use calm, positive language rather than phrases like "it won't hurt" or "no needles" that suggest fear.
  • Never use the dentist as a threat or punishment.
  • Try not to pass on your own anxiety.
  • Book a time when your child is rested and has eaten.

Our clinic has a treatment room designed specifically for children. At the first visits we take our time, introduce the surroundings and show the instruments as we explain.

AgeAdvice
First tooth – 3 yearsParent brushes twice a day with a rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste
3 – 6 yearsA pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste; brushing supervised by a parent
6 years and overChild brushes, parent checks in the evening; start the flossing habit

Cutting down how often sugary snacks are eaten is more effective than cutting the amount. See our children’s dentistry section; if crowding appears as they grow, our clear aligners vs braces comparison can help.

faq.q: When should a child have an orthodontic check?
faq.a: A first orthodontic assessment is usually recommended around age 7, when some jaw growth problems can be spotted and guided early.

faq.q: My child won't brush. What can I do?
faq.a: Making it a game, using a two-minute song or timer, and brushing alongside them helps build the habit.

faq.q: Can baby teeth have root canal treatment?
faq.a: Yes. Nerve treatment in baby teeth (pulpotomy or pulpectomy) can keep the tooth until the permanent one arrives.

faq.q: Is fluoride safe for children?
faq.a: Used in age-appropriate amounts, it's safe and effective at preventing decay. Small children use only a small amount so it isn't swallowed.

title: Implant-supported dentures: ways to stop a denture from moving
desc: What implant-supported dentures are and who they suit. Snap-on (removable) versus fixed implant dentures, how many implants are needed, care, and comparison with conventional dentures.
lead: An implant-supported denture uses two to six implants in a toothless jaw to hold the denture in place; it either clips on and off or is screwed in permanently. The movement, sore spots and chewing difficulty of a conventional denture are greatly reduced.

sections.h: What are the problems with conventional dentures?
sections.html:
• The denture moves when speaking and eating, especially in the lower jaw
  • Pressure sores on the gums
  • Much lower chewing force than natural teeth
  • Loosening over time as bone shrinks, needing frequent relines
  • The upper denture covering the palate, affecting taste and comfort

TypeTypical number of implantsFeatures
Snap-on (removable) denture2 in the lower jaw, 2–4 in the upperRemoved for cleaning; movement greatly reduced
Bar-retained denture2–4Sits on a bar joining the implants; more stable
Fixed bridge (e.g. All-on-Four)4–6Screwed in and not removed by the patient; closest to natural teeth

For details of fixed options, see our All-on-Four article.

It suits most people who have no teeth, are unhappy with their current denture and whose general health allows minor surgery. Age alone isn't a barrier. Bone is assessed with a CT scan. For health considerations, see who can get dental implants.

1. Examination, CT scan and assessment of your current denture
  2. Placing the implants (your current denture is usually adjusted and worn meanwhile)
  3. Healing: about 2–3 months in the lower jaw, 3–6 months in the upper
  4. Impressions, try-ins and fitting the new denture with its attachments
  5. Check-ups, and renewal of attachment parts when needed
Same-day loading

With suitable bone, especially for fixed full-arch solutions, the implants can carry a temporary fixed bridge on the same day. This depends on initial stability measurements.

sections.h: How do I look after it?
sections.html:
Snap-on dentures are removed and brushed daily, and the implant caps are cleaned separately. The plastic inserts in the attachments wear over time and are typically replaced every one to a few years. Fixed bridges are cleaned underneath with interdental brushes and a water flosser, with professional maintenance once or twice a year.

For general implant care, see our implant aftercare guide.

faq.q: Are two implants enough in the lower jaw?
faq.a: For a snap-on removable denture, two implants in the lower jaw markedly improve retention for most patients. A fixed bridge usually needs four or more.

faq.q: Can my existing denture be converted?
faq.a: If it's in good condition, attachments can sometimes be added to it. More often, a new denture gives a better result.

faq.q: Can I eat everything with an implant denture?
faq.a: Chewing efficiency improves markedly compared with conventional dentures. With fixed bridges an almost normal diet is possible, though very hard foods still call for care.

faq.q: Can an upper denture be made without covering the palate?
faq.a: With enough implants, upper dentures can be made without a palate, which helps taste and comfort.

title: White (composite) fillings: how they differ from amalgam and how long they last
desc: What white composite fillings are and how they compare with amalgam. When a filling is needed, how long it lasts, sensitivity afterwards, and inlays or onlays as alternatives.
lead: A white filling is made from tooth-coloured composite resin and bonded to the tooth. Compared with amalgam (silver) fillings it looks better and allows less healthy tooth to be removed; done well, it lasts for many years.

sections.html:
• When decay has reached the dentine beneath the enamel
  • For small chips and cracks
  • To replace old fillings with broken margins or decay underneath
  • For wear at the neck of the tooth due to gum recession

Early enamel decay can sometimes be halted without a filling, with fluoride and good care. That's why early diagnosis matters.

FeatureComposite (white) fillingAmalgam filling
AppearanceTooth-colouredSilver-grey
AttachmentBonded (adhesive)Mechanical retention; more tooth removed
Preserving healthy toothBetterLess
Technique sensitivityNeeds a dry field and precisionMore forgiving
Current useWidely preferredUse is declining

sections.h: Should I replace my old amalgam fillings?
sections.html: Sound amalgam fillings with intact margins and no decay underneath don't always need replacing simply because they're amalgam; removing them can also remove healthy tooth. Replacement is planned if there's a fracture, crack, leaking margin or decay, or for cosmetic reasons.

sections.h: What if the cavity is large?
sections.html: If much of the tooth is lost, a direct filling may not support it well enough. A laboratory-made inlay or onlay, or a full crown, is then considered. If decay has reached the nerve, root canal treatment may be needed first. See types of dental crowns for options.

sections.h: Sensitivity and care after a filling
sections.html:
Especially after deep fillings, sensitivity to cold can last a few days to a few weeks. If the tooth hits first when you bite, the filling may be high; a quick adjustment fixes it. Spontaneous, lingering pain may mean the nerve is affected and needs checking.

  • You can eat straight after a composite filling (once the numbness wears off).
  • Flossing matters to stop decay at the filling margins.
  • Six-monthly check-ups catch small problems early.
In short

White fillings are a cosmetic, tooth-conserving solution for small and medium cavities. For large losses of tooth structure, an inlay, onlay or crown may last longer.

faq.q: How long do white fillings last?
faq.a: Depending on size, position and oral hygiene, they usually last many years. Large fillings and grinding can shorten their life.

faq.q: Will I feel pain during a filling?
faq.a: Local anaesthetic is used when needed, so no pain is expected. Small, shallow cavities may not need anaesthetic.

faq.q: Do white fillings change colour?
faq.a: Slight surface staining can occur over time and is mostly removed by polishing. Darkening at the margins can signal leakage and should be checked.

faq.q: When can I eat after a filling?
faq.a: Composite is hardened with a light, so you can eat straight away. If you had anaesthetic, wait for the numbness to wear off so you don't bite your tongue or cheek.

title: Sensitivity, pain and care after dental crowns: what's normal?
desc: How long sensitivity lasts after a crown, whether pain is normal, what to watch for with temporary crowns, bite height, the gum margin and long-term care of crowns.
lead: Sensitivity to hot and cold and slight gum tenderness are common in the first days after a crown and usually settle within a few days to a few weeks. A high bite, or pain that increases or throbs, should be checked.

sections.html:
• Hot and cold sensitivity: Especially in vital teeth, this can last a few days to a few weeks.
  • Gum tenderness: The gum is affected during preparation and impressions, so mild soreness for a few days is common.
  • Feeling different: Your tongue takes a few days to adjust to new surfaces; speech may feel slightly different.
  • Getting used to the look: Especially when many teeth are crowned, it can take time to get used to your new smile.

sections.h: When should you contact the clinic?
sections.html:
SymptomPossible cause
That tooth hits first when you biteHigh bite; fixed with a quick adjustment
Throbbing pain that wakes you at nightNerve inflammation; root canal treatment may be needed
The crown is loose or has come offCement failure or a problem with the tooth underneath
Persistent bleeding or swelling at the gum linePoor marginal fit or gum inflammation
Sensitivity that gets worse after weeksNeeds a detailed examination
Good to know

Rarely, the nerve of a vital tooth can become inflamed some time after a crown, needing root canal treatment. This doesn't mean the crown was poorly made; it's linked to the tooth's history of decay and fillings.

sections.h: What to watch with temporary crowns
sections.html:
Temporary crowns, worn between the impression and the final crown, protect the tooth and maintain your appearance, but they aren't as strong as the final ones.

  • Avoid sticky (chewing gum, toffee) and very hard foods.
  • When flossing, slide the floss out sideways rather than pulling it up.
  • If a temporary comes off, keep it and call the clinic; an uncovered tooth can shift if left too long.

• Brush twice a day and floss or use interdental brushes daily
  • Pay attention to cleaning the crown margins (where decay most often starts)
  • A check-up and professional clean every six months
  • A night guard if you grind
  • Don't bite hard objects such as seeds, ice or pens

See our article on teeth grinding and types of dental crowns.

sections.h: Can crowns cause odour or decay underneath?
sections.html: Well-fitting, well-cleaned crowns shouldn't cause odour. Bad breath can be a sign of decay at the crown margin or gum inflammation. Read our guide to bleeding and receding gums, and if in doubt, book a check-up.

faq.q: How long does sensitivity last after a crown?
faq.a: For most people it fades over a few days to two or three weeks. If it gets worse or turns into spontaneous pain, it needs checking.

faq.q: Can I eat straight after a crown is fitted?
faq.a: You can eat once the numbness has worn off. Depending on the cement used, you may be given extra advice for the first few hours.

faq.q: Does sensitive toothpaste help?
faq.a: Yes, toothpastes with potassium nitrate or similar ingredients can help reduce temporary sensitivity.

faq.q: What should I do if a crown falls out?
faq.a: Keep the crown and call the clinic. Don't try to glue it back yourself; both the tooth and the crown can be damaged.

title: Can people with diabetes, smokers or older adults get dental implants?
desc: Who can and can't have dental implants? Implants with diabetes, smoking, older age, high blood pressure, heart conditions, blood thinners and osteoporosis medication.
lead: There's no upper age limit for implants: most adults whose general health allows minor surgery and who have enough bone can have them. Uncontrolled diabetes, heavy smoking and some medications increase the risk and need careful assessment.

sections.html:
• Jaw growth complete (usually 18 or over)
  • Enough bone to hold the implant, or bone that can be built up
  • No active infection or untreated gum disease
  • General health suitable for minor surgery under local anaesthetic
  • Commitment to oral hygiene and check-ups afterwards

sections.h: Can people with diabetes have implants?
sections.html:
People whose blood sugar is well controlled can have implants, with success rates close to those without diabetes. With uncontrolled diabetes, wound healing slows and the risk of infection rises.

That's why a recent HbA1c result is requested during planning and, where needed, we coordinate with your doctor. On the day of surgery, keep to your usual meals and medication.

Practical tip

Bringing your latest HbA1c result to the examination speeds up planning.

Yes, but smoking significantly increases the risk of the implant failing to fuse and of later inflammation around it (peri-implantitis). The more you smoke, the higher the risk. Stopping for at least a few days before surgery and throughout healing improves the odds. See our aftercare guide for post-surgery advice.

Age alone isn't a barrier; many patients have implants in their seventies and eighties. What matters is general health, medication and bone. For people with no teeth whose dentures move, securing the denture on a few implants can greatly improve quality of life. See implant-supported dentures.

sections.h: Which conditions and medications need special assessment?
sections.html:
ConditionWhat's checked
Blood thinnersNever stopped without your doctor's advice; most procedures can go ahead with dose management
Osteoporosis medicationThe type, duration and route of drugs such as bisphosphonates are reviewed
High blood pressure and heart conditionsUsually not a barrier if well controlled; current status is assessed
Radiotherapy to the head and neckBone healing may be affected, so detailed planning is needed
PregnancyElective surgery is usually postponed until after birth

Bring a list of all your medications to the examination. If needed, we'll consult your doctor.

sections.h: Can people with little bone have implants?
sections.html: In most cases, yes. Options include bone grafts, sinus lifts, or short and angled implants. See bone grafts and sinus lifts. To find out whether implants are right for you, book an examination.

faq.q: Is there an age limit for implants?
faq.a: The lower limit is when jaw growth is complete (usually 18). There's no upper limit; general health is what counts.

faq.q: I have high blood pressure. Can I have an implant?
faq.a: If it's controlled with medication, usually yes. Take your medication as normal on the day, and your blood pressure will be checked before the procedure.

faq.q: Do e-cigarettes affect implants too?
faq.a: Nicotine narrows blood vessels and can impair healing. It's best to avoid nicotine products during healing as well.

faq.q: Can I have an implant if I have gum disease?
faq.a: Gum disease is treated first. Uncontrolled gum disease raises the risk of inflammation around implants too.

title: When should wisdom teeth come out? Symptoms, procedure and recovery
desc: Do wisdom teeth always need removing? Symptoms of impacted wisdom teeth, the extraction procedure, pain and swelling, aftercare and recovery time.
lead: Wisdom teeth that have come through properly, can be cleaned and cause no problems don't need to be removed. Extraction is recommended for repeated gum infections, decay, damage to the neighbouring tooth or cysts.

sections.h: Why do wisdom teeth cause problems?
sections.html:
Wisdom teeth are the last to come through, usually between 17 and 25. When there isn't enough room in the jaw, they may stay partly or fully in the bone or gum (impacted) or tilt against the neighbouring tooth.

The flap of gum over a partly erupted tooth traps food and is hard to clean, leading to repeated inflammation (pericoronitis).

• Repeated pain, swelling and gum inflammation at the back of the mouth
  • Difficulty opening the mouth
  • Bad taste or bad breath
  • Decay in the wisdom tooth or the tooth in front of it
  • A cyst or root damage to the neighbouring tooth on X-ray
No symptoms?

Impacted wisdom teeth without symptoms can be monitored if the X-ray shows no risk. The decision weighs age, the tooth's position and possible risks.

A panoramic X-ray, and a CT scan if needed, shows the tooth's position and its proximity to the lower jaw nerve. The procedure is done under local anaesthetic.

SituationProcedure
Fully eruptedSimilar to a normal extraction, usually quick
Partly impactedThe gum is opened, the tooth sectioned if needed and removed, then stitched
Fully impacted (in bone)Surgical extraction; a small window is made in the bone

• Bite on the gauze for 30–45 minutes.
  • Apply cold to the cheek on and off on the first day.
  • For the first 24 hours avoid vigorous rinsing, spitting and straws.
  • Don't smoke; it can dislodge the clot and cause a painful "dry socket".
  • Eat soft, lukewarm food and avoid hot drinks on the first day.
  • Brush from the next day, being gentle around the extraction site.

This advice is similar to our implant aftercare guide, where you'll find more detail.

Swelling usually peaks on day 2–3 and reduces noticeably within a week. Stitches are removed after 7–10 days or dissolve. The bone takes a few months to fill in completely, but most people are back to normal within a few days.

When to call

Call the clinic if pain increases after day 3 (possible dry socket), bleeding won't stop, you develop a fever, or lip or tongue numbness hasn't gone by the next day.

At Dent32 we plan wisdom tooth extraction with X-rays and, when needed, a CT scan. For a painful wisdom tooth, see our emergency toothache guide, or book an appointment at our clinic, open seven days a week.

faq.q: Does wisdom tooth removal hurt?
faq.a: It's done under local anaesthetic, so no pain is expected during the procedure; you may feel pressure. Pain and swelling for a few days afterwards are controlled with painkillers.

faq.q: Can upper and lower wisdom teeth be removed together?
faq.a: Yes, upper and lower wisdom teeth on the same side can often be removed in one visit. Removing all four is planned case by case.

faq.q: Do wisdom teeth cause crowding?
faq.a: Wisdom teeth aren't the only cause of front-tooth crowding. Their status is assessed separately when orthodontic treatment is planned.

faq.q: How soon can I go back to work?
faq.a: After a simple extraction, usually the next day; after surgical extraction, usually 1–3 days.

title: What is dental bonding? Cosmetic correction without drilling
desc: What composite bonding is, who it suits, whether teeth are drilled and how long it lasts. Bonding versus porcelain veneers, and aftercare tips.
lead: Bonding is a cosmetic procedure in which tooth-coloured composite resin is applied to the tooth in layers and shaped. Often little or no tooth structure is removed and it's completed in one visit; it costs less than porcelain veneers but is less resistant to staining and wear.

sections.html: The tooth surface is lightly roughened, a bonding agent is applied, and tooth-coloured composite resin is built up in layers and hardened with a curing light. It's then shaped and polished. It usually takes 30–60 minutes per tooth and often needs no anaesthetic.

• Small chips and cracks on front teeth
  • Small gaps between teeth (diastema)
  • Short or misshapen teeth
  • Localised stains that whitening can't lift
  • Exposed root surfaces due to gum recession

FeatureBonding (composite)Porcelain veneer
Tooth reductionUsually none or minimalUsually 0.3–0.7 mm
VisitsUsually one2–3 (impression and laboratory)
Colour stabilityCan stain over time with tea and coffeeDoesn't change colour
DurabilityEdges can chip and wearMore durable
RepairEasily repaired in the mouthUsually replaced if broken
CostLowerHigher

For details on porcelain veneers, see our laminate veneer article.

Depending on care and habits, bonding usually lasts several years up to around ten. Polishing and small repairs may be needed along the way. Nail biting, chewing pens and grinding shorten its life.

Tip

If you're also considering whitening, whiten first and do the bonding once the shade has settled (usually after 2 weeks). Composite doesn't whiten.

• Avoid strongly coloured food and drinks (coffee, tea, red wine, cola) for the first 48 hours
  • Brush and floss regularly
  • Have the surface polished at check-ups
  • Don't bite hard objects with your front teeth

For a more comprehensive change, options are assessed together through smile design. For tooth colour, see our teeth whitening guide.

faq.q: Are teeth drilled for bonding?
faq.a: In most cases no drilling is needed, or only light roughening of the surface. That makes bonding one of the most reversible cosmetic options.

faq.q: Does bonding turn yellow?
faq.a: Composite can pick up stains from tea, coffee and smoking over time. Regular polishing helps keep the colour.

faq.q: Does bonding hurt?
faq.a: It usually needs no anaesthetic and is painless. Local anaesthetic can be used for sensitive areas.

faq.q: Can gaps between teeth be closed with bonding?
faq.a: Small and moderate gaps can often be closed with bonding. For large gaps or crowding, orthodontics is assessed first.

title: Does professional teeth cleaning damage enamel? How often should you have it?
desc: What tartar is and why it forms. Whether scaling damages enamel or creates gaps, whether it hurts, how often it's needed, sensitivity afterwards and home care.
lead: Professional cleaning (scaling) removes hardened bacterial plaque from the teeth with ultrasonic instruments. Done properly, it doesn't damage enamel; most people need it every six months, and people with gum disease more often.

sections.html:
Bacterial plaque forms on teeth all the time. Plaque that isn't removed by brushing and flossing combines with minerals in saliva and starts to harden within days, turning into tartar. It builds up most on the inner surfaces of the lower front teeth and the cheek side of the upper molars, where the salivary glands open.

Tartar's rough surface holds more plaque and fuels gum inflammation. Once formed, it can't be brushed off.

No. Ultrasonic instruments break up tartar with vibration and wash it away with a water spray; used correctly, they don't wear enamel. The feeling that gaps have "opened up" afterwards is actually the spaces that tartar was filling. Teeth don't move apart; as inflammation settles, the gums recover.

A common myth

"Scaling makes teeth loose" isn't true. Looseness is caused by bone loss from tartar left for a long time. Cleaning stops that process.

sections.h: How is it done, and does it hurt?
sections.html:
1. Examination and X-rays if needed
  2. Removing tartar with ultrasonic instruments
  3. Cleaning delicate areas with hand instruments
  4. Removing stains and polishing

It usually takes 30–45 minutes. Without gum inflammation, most people feel only mild discomfort. For sensitivity, local anaesthetic or desensitising treatments can be used.

sections.h: How often should you have it?
sections.html:
SituationRecommended frequency
Healthy gums, little tartarEvery 6–12 months
Fast tartar build-up, smokersUsually every 6 months
After gum disease treatmentEvery 3–4 months
Implants or many crownsEvery 6 months, with a check-up

For a few days afterwards there may be sensitivity to cold and slight gum bleeding; this usually settles by itself, and sensitive toothpaste helps. Cleaning also reduces tea and coffee stains; lightening the teeth's natural colour is a separate procedure, teeth whitening.

For more on bleeding and receding gums, see our gum health guide.

faq.q: Does scaling whiten teeth?
faq.a: It removes tartar and surface stains from tea, coffee and smoking, so teeth look cleaner and brighter, but it doesn't change the teeth's natural colour.

faq.q: Can I remove tartar at home?
faq.a: No. Tartar can't be safely removed with a toothbrush or home tools. What you can do at home is prevent it with regular brushing and flossing.

faq.q: Is scaling safe during pregnancy?
faq.a: Yes, and it's recommended to keep gum inflammation under control. The second trimester is usually the most comfortable time.

faq.q: Is a clean included in a check-up?
faq.a: It depends on the clinic and your needs. At Dent32 we tell you at the examination whether a clean is needed and what it involves.

title: Teeth clenching and grinding (bruxism): symptoms and night guards
desc: What bruxism is and why it happens. Symptoms such as morning jaw pain and tooth wear, how a night guard is made, and other treatments including Botox.
lead: Bruxism is clenching or grinding the teeth without realising, during the day or in sleep. It can cause tooth wear, chips and cracks, damage to crowns and jaw pain; the most common protection is a custom-made night guard.

sections.html:
• Pain or tiredness in the jaw, temples or facial muscles on waking
  • Morning headaches
  • Flattened, worn teeth and chipped enamel
  • Increased sensitivity to cold
  • Clicking in the jaw or difficulty opening the mouth
  • A partner noticing grinding noises at night

There's no single cause. Stress and anxiety, sleep disorders (especially snoring and sleep apnoea), caffeine, alcohol, smoking and some medications can increase the risk. Daytime clenching usually happens unconsciously during concentration or stress.

sections.h: What is a night guard and how is it made?
sections.html:
A night guard is a clear, rigid appliance made to fit your upper or lower teeth from an impression or digital scan. It doesn't stop grinding entirely, but it takes the force instead of your teeth, protecting them and any restorations and balancing the muscle load.

TypeFeatures
Over-the-counter guardsCheap but poor fit; not recommended long term
Soft custom guardComfortable, but can increase the chewing reflex in some people
Hard custom guardThe bite can be balanced; the most common choice for bruxism
Crowns and implants

For people with zirconia, e.max or implant crowns who grind, a night guard is especially important to protect their restorations.

• Awareness: Notice during the day whether your teeth are touching; at rest, with lips closed, teeth should be slightly apart.
  • Muscle relaxation: Jaw exercises, warm compresses, physiotherapy.
  • Botulinum toxin (Botox): After assessment, can be used in some patients to reduce excessive contraction of the chewing muscles; its effect is temporary.
  • Sleep assessment: Referral to a specialist if snoring or sleep apnoea is suspected.
  • Repairing damaged teeth: Worn teeth are restored with fillings, bonding or crowns.

Rinse the guard with cold or lukewarm water every morning, clean it with a soft brush and store it dry in its case. Don't use hot water, which can warp it. Bring it to your check-ups. For restoring worn teeth, see types of dental crowns and dental bonding.

A night guard is different from orthodontic aligners: it doesn't move teeth, it only protects them. For aligners, see clear aligners or braces.

faq.q: Will a night guard stop me grinding?
faq.a: Not always, but it protects teeth and restorations from wear and can reduce the load on the muscles.

faq.q: How long does a night guard last?
faq.a: Depending on how hard you grind, usually several years. It's replaced if it wears through, cracks or no longer fits.

faq.q: Is grinding normal in children?
faq.a: Night grinding is common with baby teeth and often decreases on its own. If there's pain, marked wear or sleep problems, it should be assessed.

faq.q: Can someone having aligner treatment use a night guard?
faq.a: Aligners protect the teeth to some extent during treatment. If grinding continues afterwards, a retainer and night guard can be planned together.

title: What is smile design and who is it for?
desc: What smile design is, which treatments it can include, who it suits, how the trial stage works and what affects the cost.
lead: Smile design is a planning method that sets the length, shape and colour of the teeth and the gum line according to your facial proportions, and lets you see the result before treatment begins.

sections.h: What exactly does smile design involve?
sections.html:
Smile design is not a single procedure but a way of planning. First, your face, lips and teeth are examined as a whole: how much tooth shows when you talk and smile, your facial midline, the gum level and the proportions between teeth.

This is recorded with photos, video and an intraoral scan. The intended result is then designed digitally. The design works like a prescription: it shows which tooth needs which treatment — and where nothing should be done at all.

sections.h: Who is it suitable for, and who is it not?
sections.html:
Smile design usually makes sense for people with more than one aesthetic concern who want to solve them in a single plan:

  • The length, shape or colour of the teeth looks out of balance with the face
  • There are gaps, chips or worn edges
  • Too much gum shows when smiling, or the gum line is uneven
  • Old crowns and fillings no longer match in colour

Untreated decay, gum disease or a significant bite problem must be dealt with first. An aesthetic plan is built on a healthy foundation.

sections.h: How does the process work, step by step?
sections.html:
The table below gives a general framework. The exact timeline depends on which treatments the plan includes and is set after the examination.

StageWhat happensTypical time
Examination and recordsClinical exam, X-rays, photos, video and scan1 appointment
Digital designPlanning target tooth length, shape and proportionsA few days
Trial (mock-up)Trying the design in the mouth with temporary material1 appointment
TreatmentTreatments according to the approved planDepends on the treatment chosen
ReviewFit, bite and maintenance check1 appointment
Why the trial stage matters

With a mock-up you see the result on your own face, in the mirror. Any detail you don't like is changed before anything permanent is done.

sections.h: Which treatments can be part of smile design?
sections.html:
The plan is shaped around you. For some patients whitening and a little bonding are enough; others need a combination of treatments:

  • Teeth whitening: to lighten natural teeth
  • Orthodontics / clear aligners: to align crowded teeth without reducing them
  • Laminate veneers: thin porcelain layers to change shape and colour
  • Zirconia crowns: for teeth with more tissue loss
  • Gum contouring: to balance the gum line

Smile design does not always mean reducing teeth. The least invasive option that preserves the natural tooth should always be considered first.

There is no single price for smile design; the cost follows the content of the plan. Getting an itemised written plan after the examination is the soundest way to compare.

FactorEffect on cost
Number of teeth treatedA plan for 6, 8 or 10 visible teeth costs differently
Material chosenVeneers, zirconia or bonding differ in cost and lifespan
Preliminary treatmentOrthodontics, gum treatment or decay treatment may be needed
Laboratory and digital workflowCustom design and trial stages are part of the plan

faq.q: Is smile design painful?
faq.a: The design and trial stages are painless. Treatments that require tooth preparation are done under local anaesthetic; there may be short-term sensitivity afterwards.

faq.q: Can I see the result in advance?
faq.a: Yes. With the digital design and an in-mouth trial (mock-up), you see the result on your own face before any permanent work.

faq.q: Do my teeth have to be reduced?
faq.a: No. The plan may consist of non-invasive treatments such as whitening, orthodontics or bonding. If reduction is needed, the reason and amount are explained before starting.

faq.q: How long does the result last?
faq.a: It depends on the treatments used, oral hygiene and habits. Porcelain restorations can last many years; regular check-ups extend their life.

title: All-on-Four: are fixed teeth on four implants really possible?
desc: What All-on-Four is, who it suits and whether same-day fixed teeth are possible. The process, risks, limitations and cost factors.
lead: All-on-Four is a treatment in which a fixed full-arch prosthesis is placed on four implants in a jaw that has no teeth or is about to lose them.

sections.html:
In a conventional approach, six to eight implants may be planned for a full jaw. All-on-Four uses four: the two front implants are placed upright and the two back implants at an angle.

The angled back implants take support from areas where the bone is denser. This keeps them away from the sinus in the upper jaw and the nerve in the lower jaw, which reduces the need for bone grafting in many patients.

• People missing all teeth in one jaw
  • People whose remaining teeth cannot be saved because of advanced gum disease
  • Denture wearers who want fixed teeth
  • Patients whose CT scan shows enough bone for four implants

Uncontrolled diabetes, heavy smoking, a history of head and neck radiotherapy and certain bone medications increase the risk. These should be discussed in detail at the examination.

If the implants achieve enough initial stability (primary stability) in the bone, most patients can have a temporary fixed prosthesis fitted the same day or within a few days, so you are not left without teeth while healing.

The temporary prosthesis is used until the bone has fused with the implants. A soft diet is needed in the first weeks. The final prosthesis is made from new impressions after healing.

Note

If initial stability is not sufficient, the dentist may let the implants heal without load. This decision is made during surgery, based on the bone.

sections.h: How are the process and timeline planned?
sections.html:
StageTypical time
Examination and 3D CT scan1–2 appointments
Any extractions, implant surgery and temporary fixed prosthesisUsually the same day or within a few days
Healing and bone integrationAbout 3–6 months
Making and fitting the final prosthesisSeveral appointments
Check-ups and professional cleaningAt least 1–2 times a year

These are general ranges; they vary with bone quality and general health.

sections.h: What are the risks and limitations?
sections.html:
When well planned, All-on-Four is a predictable treatment, but like any implant treatment it carries risks:

  • An implant failing to integrate with the bone (more common with smoking and uncontrolled diabetes)
  • Inflammation around implants (peri-implantitis), mostly linked to inadequate cleaning
  • Fracture or wear of the prosthesis in people who clench or grind at night
  • The prosthesis needing maintenance or renewal in the long term

The underside of a fixed prosthesis must be cleaned too. Interdental brushes and a water flosser should be part of the daily routine, as your dentist will show you.

FactorExplanation
Implant systemClinical evidence and long-term parts availability matter
Final prosthesis materialAcrylic, composite or zirconia differ in cost and durability
Additional proceduresExtractions or limited bone grafting may be needed
One or two jawsEach jaw is planned separately

faq.q: Can four implants carry all the teeth?
faq.a: With suitable bone and correct planning, yes. Angled back implants spread the load over a wider area. If bone is insufficient, more implants may be recommended.

faq.q: Will the surgery hurt?
faq.a: It is done under local anaesthetic; sedation can be discussed if you wish. Swelling and tenderness may follow for a few days and are managed with prescribed medication.

faq.q: Can I eat normally with temporary teeth?
faq.a: A soft diet is recommended for the first weeks. Hard and sticky food can overload the implants until the bone has integrated.

faq.q: Can the All-on-Four prosthesis be removed?
faq.a: Not by the patient. Because it is screw-retained, the dentist can remove it for cleaning at check-ups.

faq.q: Is All-on-Four suitable for everyone?
faq.a: No. A decision can't be made without a CT scan and an assessment of general health and bone volume. For some patients a conventional implant plan is better.

title: What are laminate veneers, are teeth reduced, and how long do they last?
desc: What laminate veneers are, how much tooth is reduced, who they suit and how long they last. Comparison with zirconia and the process.
lead: A laminate veneer is a thin layer of porcelain, usually 0.3–0.7 mm thick, bonded only to the front surface of a tooth.

sections.html:
In most cases a very thin layer of enamel is removed from the front of the tooth, usually less than half a millimetre. The aim is for the porcelain to create a natural profile without bulging.

In some cases — for example when teeth are small or set back — veneers can be placed without any reduction (no-prep). But this does not suit every tooth and can lead to a bulky look and gum problems.

Important

Removed enamel does not grow back. The decision for veneers should be made after alternatives (whitening, orthodontics, bonding) have been discussed.

• Discolouration that does not respond to whitening
  • Small chips and wear on front teeth
  • Small gaps between teeth
  • Mismatched shape and length

With severe crowding, heavy clenching or when most of the tooth is missing, veneers may not be a good option. In those cases orthodontics or crowns are considered.

FeatureLaminate veneerZirconia crown
CoverageFront surface of the toothAll surfaces of the tooth
Tooth tissue removedLittleMore
Suitable forSound front teeth without large fillingsWeakened, root-treated or fractured teeth
TranslucencyVery highHigh

In short, veneers are for teeth that are structurally sound and whose appearance you mainly want to change. If a tooth is weakened, a crown protects it better.

Studies report that most porcelain veneers placed for the right indication with good bonding technique remain in place for ten years or more.

The main factors that shorten their life are night-time clenching, nail biting or biting hard objects, poor oral hygiene and gum recession. If you clench, a night guard is recommended.

StageWhat happensTypical time
PlanningPhotos, scan and smile design1 appointment
TrialTrying the design temporarily in the mouth1 appointment
Preparation and impressionsAny minimal reduction and impressions1 appointment
BondingPermanent bonding after colour and fit checks1 appointment

Including laboratory time, the process is usually completed within one to two weeks.

FactorExplanation
Number of teethPlanned according to how many teeth show in your smile
Porcelain type and laboratoryLayered or monolithic porcelain, hand finishing
Preliminary treatmentWhitening, gum contouring or orthodontics may be needed

faq.q: Will my teeth be sensitive after veneers?
faq.a: There may be short-term sensitivity. Because reduction stays within the enamel, lasting sensitivity is rare.

faq.q: Do veneers change colour?
faq.a: Porcelain does not stain or change colour. Natural teeth can darken over time, so if whitening is needed it is done before the veneers.

faq.q: Can a veneer come off?
faq.a: It is rare when bonded correctly. Biting hard objects and clenching increase the risk.

faq.q: Can veneers be removed so I go back to my old teeth?
faq.a: If teeth were reduced, the surface does not return to its original state; the tooth should always be protected by a restoration. This is worth knowing before you decide.

title: Teeth whitening: in the clinic or at home? How long does it last?
desc: The differences between in-clinic and at-home whitening, how long results last, sensitivity and cases where whitening doesn't work.
lead: Teeth whitening is a dentist-supervised procedure that lightens tooth colour by breaking down pigments in the enamel and dentine with peroxide-based gels.

sections.h: What is the difference between in-clinic and at-home whitening?
sections.html:
Both methods use the same active ingredient; the difference is gel concentration and application time.

MethodHow it's appliedTypical timeWho it suits
In-clinic (in-office)Gums are protected; a high-concentration gel is applied by the dentistOne session, about 1–1.5 hoursThose who want a quick result
At home (with trays)Low-concentration gel in custom-made traysUsually 1–2 weeks of daily useThose who want gradual, controlled lightening
CombinedStart in the clinic, continue at homeOne clinic session + short home useThose who want a more pronounced, even result

Over-the-counter products are usually very low in concentration, and because the trays aren't custom-made the gel can reach the gums. Dentist-supervised whitening gives more predictable results.

The result is not permanent; teeth gradually pick up colour again. How quickly depends on habits. Tea, coffee, red wine and smoking bring the colour back faster.

Most patients notice the effect for one to several years. If you keep your home trays, short top-up applications can be done on your dentist's advice.

sections.h: Does it cause sensitivity or damage enamel?
sections.html:
Temporary sensitivity is a common side effect and usually settles on its own within a few days. Desensitising toothpaste and adjusting application intervals help.

Studies have shown that whitening at recommended concentrations under a dentist's supervision does not permanently damage enamel. The real risk is uncontrolled, excessive use.

Examination first

Decay, exposed root surfaces or leaking fillings can make whitening painful. That's why an examination and scale-and-polish come first.

• Crowns, fillings and veneers: restorations don't whiten, so a colour mismatch may appear afterwards.
  • Some medication-related staining: for example, tetracycline stains respond only partly.
  • Dark root-treated teeth: special internal whitening may be needed.

In these cases options such as veneers or crowns are discussed.

sections.h: What should I watch out for after whitening?
sections.html:
• Avoid tea, coffee, cola, red wine and coloured sauces for the first 48 hours.
  • Try not to smoke during this time.
  • If teeth are sensitive, cut down on very hot and very cold food for a few days.
  • Check-ups and cleaning every six months help keep the colour.

faq.q: How many shades lighter will my teeth get?
faq.a: It depends on the starting colour and type of staining. Yellowish teeth usually respond well; greyish discolouration lightens less.

faq.q: Can I whiten my teeth while pregnant?
faq.a: Whitening is not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding; it is best postponed until afterwards.

faq.q: Is whitening painful?
faq.a: No pain is expected during the procedure. Some patients have temporary sensitivity and brief twinges.

faq.q: Will my crowns whiten too?
faq.a: No. Porcelain and zirconia restorations don't change colour. If you have restorations on front teeth, colour matching should be planned in advance.

title: Travelling to Istanbul for dental treatment: a planning guide
desc: Coming to Istanbul for dental treatment from abroad: what to send in advance, how long to stay, planning the trip and aftercare at home.
lead: If you are thinking of coming to Istanbul from abroad for dental treatment, the most important step is to settle the treatment plan and length of stay before you book a flight.

sections.h: What should I send before I come?
sections.html:
The more detailed the preliminary assessment, the more realistic the plan. You can send the following via WhatsApp:

  • A panoramic X-ray taken within the last 6 months (and a CT scan if you have one)
  • Clear photos of your teeth from the front, the side and while smiling
  • Any medication you take and chronic conditions
  • Your expectations: what you want to change and what bothers you

With this, the dentist prepares a preliminary plan. The final plan can only be confirmed after an examination and imaging at the clinic — it's important to know this before you travel.

sections.h: How long will I need to stay?
sections.html:
The length of stay varies a lot by treatment. The figures below are general ranges:

TreatmentFirst visitSecond visit
Zirconia / veneersAbout 5–7 daysUsually not needed
Implants (final teeth later)2–5 daysAfter 3–6 months, about 5–7 days
All-on-FourAbout 5–7 days (temporary fixed teeth)After 3–6 months, for the final prosthesis
Teeth whitening1–2 daysNot needed
Clear aligners1–3 days to startRemote follow-up + periodic check-ups
Flexible return

Book a flexible return flight if you can. Small adjustments at the trial stage may need a day or two more.

sections.h: How should I plan the trip?
sections.html:
Dent32 is in Beylikdüzü, on the European side of Istanbul. Staying on the European side makes clinic visits easier; Istanbul Airport is closer to this area than Sabiha Gökçen.

  • If you are having surgery, don't plan a busy sightseeing day for the same day.
  • Ask your dentist about flight timing after implant surgery or extractions.
  • Alcohol and smoking slow healing on treatment days.
  • Bring any medication you take regularly.

sections.h: How does follow-up work once I'm home?
sections.html:
Your X-rays and records are given to you after treatment, so your dentist at home can see what was done. During healing, you can reach your dentist via WhatsApp by sending photos with your questions.

In the long run, most of the success depends on maintenance. A check-up and professional cleaning at least once a year should not be skipped, wherever it is done.

Comparing quotes from different clinics on the total figure alone can be misleading. Ask these questions:

TopicQuestion to ask
MaterialsWhich implant brand, and which type of zirconia or porcelain, will be used?
ScopeAre X-rays, CT scans, temporary teeth and check-ups included?
Number of teethWhich teeth does the plan cover, and why?
AlternativesIs there a less invasive option?

faq.q: Can I communicate in English?
faq.a: Yes. You can communicate in English during the preliminary assessment and appointment process.

faq.q: Can I get a firm price from photos?
faq.a: Photos and X-rays allow preliminary information; the final plan and cost are confirmed after the examination at the clinic.

faq.q: Can I have the implant and the final tooth in the same visit?
faq.a: In most cases, no. The implant needs a few months to integrate with the bone. In some cases temporary fixed teeth can be fitted.

faq.q: How far in advance should I book?
faq.a: Complete the preliminary assessment before booking flights, then agree dates with the clinic so treatment days fit your trip.

faq.q: What if there's a problem after treatment?
faq.a: Send photos and a description via WhatsApp. The dentist will assess the situation and advise you.

title: Clear aligners or braces? The real differences between them
desc: Clear aligners versus fixed braces: appearance, comfort, suitable cases, treatment time and retention afterwards.
lead: Clear aligners and fixed braces are two orthodontic methods for straightening teeth; both are effective, but they differ in appearance, the discipline they require and the cases they suit.

sections.html:
FeatureClear alignersFixed braces
VisibilityAlmost invisibleVisible (clear brackets are an option)
RemovabilityRemoved for eating and brushingFixed; removed by the orthodontist
Patient complianceMust be worn 20–22 hours a dayDoesn't depend on the patient wearing them
Oral hygieneBrushing is easyBrackets need extra care
Food restrictionsFew, since aligners come outAvoid hard and sticky food
Complex casesCan be limitedWider control of tooth movement

sections.h: When are braces the better choice?
sections.html:
Clear aligners have improved a great deal and work well in many cases. Even so, fixed braces are more predictable in some situations:

  • Severe crowding or cases that require extractions
  • Cases needing significant vertical tooth movement
